newsitem.title: ISRAEL: ORBOTECH SETS AMBITIOUS SALES TARGET.
newsitem.headline: ORBOTECH SETS AMBITIOUS SALES TARGET.

text.p: Orbotech Ltd of Israel is striving to double annual sales to $300 million by the end of the decade by investing in research and development and through acquisitions, company officials said on Thursday.
Vice President for marketing and business development Haim Shani would not disclose the company's sales and profit forecast for next year.
"We expect growth will continue next year. We hope we won't disappoint," he told reporters.
Orbotech is one of the stars of Israel's high tech-industry. Its shares have soared more than 180 percent this year and are on the buy list of many Wall Street analysts.
Earlier this week Orbotech announced second quarter net profit of $8.5 million, or $0.62 a share, up 73 percent from a year earlier and well above analysts' expectations.
Revenues grew 27 percent to $46.4 million, while net margins rose to 18.3 percent from 13.4 percent.
Oppenheimer & Co forecast Orbotech will earn $2.40 a share in 1997 and $2.80 in 1998 against last year's $1.54, excluding a one-time gain from the sale of its holdings in Opal Inc.
Orbotech is the world leader in the manufacture of automated optical inspection systems for the printed circuit board (PCB) industry. This accounts for 78 percent of the company's sales.
"This is our bread and butter," Shani said in a presentation to analysts and reporters in Tel Aviv.
There are 3,500 PCB manufacturers and the $27 billion industry is growing seven percent a year.
The multilayer and fine line PCB sector Orbotech targets is growing eight to 10 percent a year.
Orbotech's inspection machines cost $350,000 to $750,000 each and its clients include Samsung, Goldstar, IBM and Hewlett Packard, as well as small plants in China, Taiwan and the United States.
To continue growing rapidly the company is targetting a number of other fields, as well as investing $25 million annually in R&D.

It is forging ahead with the development of laser direct imaging. In 1996, it teamed up with Germany's Jenoptik, a leader in high-end optic technology, in a joint venture for the development of direct imaging systems, which reduce manufacturing costs while providing high accuracy.
This moves the company beyond inspection and into PCB production equipment, company officials said.
"The potential sales of direct imaging equipment is $100 million a year," Shani said.
Another growing area is the manufacture of flat panel displays used in wall and projection televisions, computers, video cameras and car navigation systems.
Orbotech's sales of inspection systems for flat panel displays soared 142 percent in the second quarter. Orbotech's systems cost about $1 million.
In April, Orbotech announced the first order for its automated optical inspection system for shadow masks -- fine metal grids that are components of cathode ray tubes.
Sales of shadow masks in 1997 are projected at $1.5 billion to $2.0 billion with annual growth at eight percent.
The size of the inspection market is about $30 million a year.
Orbotech is also developing inspection systems for the production of lead frames, which are the metal component conecting silicon chips to the electronic circuitry.
-- Tova Cohen, Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211 TCC
